topic: Harappan Town Planning and Great Bath
questionText: The 'Great Bath' discovered at Mohenjo-daro was a large rectangular tank situated in a courtyard. A key architectural and waterproofing feature of the Great Bath was:

options.text: Constructing the entire tank out of imported white Carrara marble
Connecting the tank directly to the Arabian Sea via an underwater aqueduct
Lining the brick edges with gypsum mortar and using bitumen to make the tank watertight
Decorating the walls with royal dynastic relief inscriptions

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
According to NCERT Class 12 History (Bricks, Beads and Bones - Harappan Town Planning and Great Bath):
The Great Bath on the Citadel of Mohenjo-daro had steps leading down on north and south sides. It was made watertight by setting bricks on edge and using a mortar of gypsum, with rooms on three sides and a well in one room.

Hence, Option (C) is the correct answer.

questionText: According to the Brahmanical texts (Dharmashastras) on Gotra rules formulated around 1000 BCE onwards:

options.text: Women were expected to adopt their husband's gotra upon marriage, and members of the same gotra could not marry
Women retained their father's gotra throughout life in all royal dynasties
Endogamous marriage within the same gotra was compulsory across all varnas
Gotra was determined strictly matrilineally through the mother's lineage

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
According to NCERT Class 12 History (Kinship, Caste and Class - Dharmashastras and Gotra Rules):
Two main Gotra rules: (1) Women were expected to give up their father's gotra and adopt that of their husband upon marriage, and (2) Members of the same gotra could not marry (exogamy). (Note: Satavahanas were an exception where queens retained father gotras).

Hence, Option (A) is the correct answer.

topic: Ibn Battuta's Observations on Indian Postal System
questionText: In his travelogue 'Rihla', the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta marveled at the speed and efficiency of the Delhi Sultanate postal system, describing the horse post (uluq) and the foot post known as:

options.text: Barid
Dawa (stations established every one-third of a mile with swift runners)
Diwan
Muqaddam

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
According to NCERT Class 12 History (Through the Eyes of Travellers - Ibn Battuta's Observations on Indian Postal System):
Ibn Battuta observed two kinds of postal systems: the horse post, called 'uluq' (stations every four miles), and the foot post, called 'dawa' (three stations per mile with runners holding copper-belled batons), which conveyed news faster than the horse post.

Hence, Option (B) is the correct answer.

topic: Al-Biruni on the Concept of Pollution
questionText:

"Al-Biruni tried to explain the caste system by looking for parallels in other societies. In ancient Persia, he noted four classes: knights and princes; monks and fire-priests; lawyers, physicians, astronomers and other scientists; and peasants and artisans. In other words, he attempted to suggest that social divisions were not unique to India. At the same time, Al-Biruni disapproved of the Brahmanical notion of pollution. He remarked that everything which falls into a state of impurity strives and succeeds in regaining its original condition of purity. The sun cleanses the air, and the salt in the sea prevents the water from becoming foul. If it were not so, insisted Al-Biruni, life on earth would have been impossible. "Francois Bernier left a harrowing eyewitness account of the practice of Sati which he witnessed firsthand at Lahore: 'At Lahore I saw a most beautiful young widow, not more than twelve years of age, sacrificed. The poor little creature appeared more dead than alive when she approached the dreadful pit; the agony of her mind cannot be described; she trembled and wept bitterly; but three or four of the Brahmanas, assisted by an old woman who held her under the arm, forced the unhappy victim toward the pyre, seated her upon the wood, tied her hands and feet lest she should run away, and in that situation the innocent creature was burnt alive. I found it difficult to repress my feelings and to prevent their bursting forth into violent action.'"

How did Bernier describe the physical coercion exercised upon the young victim by priests and attendants?

options.text: They permitted her to walk away when she hesitated
They placed her peacefully on the pyre while she chanted hymns joyfully
They held her down under her arms, forced her onto the wood pyre, and bound her hands and feet to prevent escape
They asked the Mughal governor to grant her a royal pardon

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
According to NCERT principles for Medieval Society through Travellers Accounts (Bernier's Account of Sati at Lahore):
They held her down under her arms, forced her onto the wood pyre, and bound her hands and feet to prevent escape

Detailed Context:
1. Bernier emphasized that far from being voluntary, the child wept in terror and was forcibly tied down with logs and ropes.
Hence Option B is correct.

Therefore, option (C) is the correct answer.

Hence, Option (C) is the correct answer.

questionText:
Read the following excerpt carefully and answer the question that follows:

"Ibn Battuta set out on his travels when he was only twenty-one years old. In his travelogue Rihla, he wrote passionately: 'I set out alone, having neither fellow-traveller in whose companionship I might find cheer, nor caravan whose party I might join, but swayed by an overmastering impulse within me and a desire long-cherished in my bosom to visit these illustrious sanctuaries. So I braced my resolution to quit my dear ones, female and male, and forsook my home as birds forsake their nests... I was then twenty-two years of age.' Ibn Battuta reached Sindh in 1333, travelling via Central Asia, and made his way to Delhi where he was appointed Qazi by Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq."
